plan.title: feat(release): a maintainer cut needs only the release grant: no policy flip, no direct push, no hotfix label afterwards

narratives.Description: Today a maintainer release needs a policy switch, a commit and a direct push to master before the cut, the same again after it, and a `hotfix` label on the next PR, because the cut empties `[Unreleased]` and master's merge gate turns red. This story sends the cut through the merge queue: `task release` works on a fresh `release/v<version>` branch and opens a release PR, and a second step `task release -- --finish <version>` tags the merged commit by its SHA and pushes only the tag after its checks and the release grant. The release writes one release line back under `[Unreleased]`, so master stays green, and the changelog check uses that line to judge a release change set by a narrow release rule (release files only, matching version heading, the line alone, no note lost). `verify:changelog-unreleased` skips merge-queue runs like the other PR-context checks. The policy switch, the direct pushes, the override variables and the hotfix label leave the normal path; the old atomic push stays behind one break-glass flag, and recovery of a merged but untagged release stays break-glass until #6485.
narratives.UserStory: As a maintainer who cuts a Directive release, I want the cut to land through the merge queue as an ordinary PR and the tag to follow by one finish command, so that the release grant is my only human act and master's merge gate stays green after the release.

narratives.Overview:
1. Release branch. `task release` runs on a branch named `release/v<version>` made from the fetched tip of the base branch. Step 2 accepts that branch and refuses every other branch, the base branch included, unless the break-glass flag of item 10 is passed. Steps 3 to 9 are unchanged except for item 4. When a branch of that name already exists locally or on the remote, the cut refuses and names the recovery of item 7; it never continues on a branch from an earlier attempt.
2. Release PR. In place of Steps 10 and 11 the cut pushes the release branch and opens the release PR, then stops and prints the command of item 3. The generated PR body carries the documentation-impact declaration in the form `verify:docs-impact` accepts, the version, and no closing keyword; release notes are not copied into the body. The PR merges through the merge queue with `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` like every PR.
3. Finish step. `task release -- --finish <version>` resolves the merged release PR and its merge commit M. It refuses unless all of these hold: M is on the fetched base branch; M has one parent; the diff from that parent to M changes only `CHANGELOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md` and deleted files under `changelog.d/`; `CHANGELOG.md` at M holds the `## [<version>]` heading and the release line of that version; at M that release line is the only entry under `[Unreleased]` and `changelog.d/` holds no fragment; and the named merge gate read that Step 5 preflight already uses reports green for M. It then runs the closed-verb gate (the release grant), creates the tag on M by its SHA, pushes only the tag, and runs Steps 12 and 13 with the release notes read from `CHANGELOG.md` at M. The grant authorizes the version; it is not evidence about the commit.
4. Release line. When the release promotes `[Unreleased]`, it writes one entry line under the fresh `[Unreleased]` section. The line has one fixed form, held in one named constant: a `- ` entry that carries a fixed tag and `v<version>`. The release line of the previous release is not copied into the promoted version section; the fresh section holds exactly one release line.
5. Release rule. In merge-base mode, a change set whose `CHANGELOG.md` change adds a release line is a release attempt. A release attempt passes only when all of these hold: (a) every changed path is `CHANGELOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md` or a deleted fragment under `changelog.d/`; (b) the same change adds a `## [<version>]` heading whose version is the version in the added release line; (c) in the tree under check, the added release line is the only entry under `[Unreleased]` and `changelog.d/` holds no fragment; (d) every non-blank line of `CHANGELOG.md` at the merge base that lies above the link footer, other than a release line of an earlier version, occurs in `CHANGELOG.md` at HEAD at least as many times as at the merge base; (e) every non-blank line of every deleted fragment after its `section:` line occurs in the new version section at HEAD at least as many times as in the deleted fragments together. For (d) and (e) a line is compared after CRLF is read as LF and trailing whitespace is removed; no entry parser is used. A passing release attempt needs no other new entry. A failing release attempt fails the check; it is never judged by the ordinary rules. A change set that removes or changes a release line without adding one fails. Every other change set is judged by today's rules, and the release line already in the file does not count as its entry.
6. Where the check runs. `verify:changelog-unreleased` joins the PR-context checks that skip themselves on a `merge_group` run and print the existing skip notice. What is given up is stated in the docs: on a merge-queue commit nothing re-checks the changelog; the entry requirement and the release rule were judged on the PR at its last CI run.
7. Changes that land ahead. Case A: a PR that adds a fragment or an `[Unreleased]` entry merges to the base branch before the release PR's check runs. Condition (c) of item 5 fails on the release PR. Recovery: close the release PR, delete the release branch, and run the cut again; it makes a fresh release branch from the new tip. Case B: such a PR is still in the merge queue ahead of the release PR and lands first. Item 6 means no check sees it; the finish step refuses by item 3 and names the leftover entries or fragments. Undoing that untagged release is not part of this story: it uses the break-glass path of item 10 until #6485 ships, and the docs say so.
8. Master after a release. The empty-section rule of `verify:changelog-unreleased` is not changed. The release line is the entry that keeps `[Unreleased]` non-empty at the release commit.
9. Docs. `docs/RELEASING.md` and the release skill state the release PR path, the finish step, the release line, items 6 and 7, and recovery by state. PR open: close the PR and delete the release branch, or run the cut again. Merged and not tagged: run the finish step; to abandon, revert the release commit with a PR through the queue. Tagged: `task release:rollback`, which is unchanged, still pushes the base branch directly and needs an operator with ruleset bypass. The Branch-Protection Policy Guard steps and the policy switch and restore block leave the normal path.
10. Break-glass. The existing run on the base branch with the atomic push stays behind one explicit flag, documented under the break-glass heading only. It writes the release line too.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a minted release grant, when a maintainer runs the cut and the finish step, then `plan.policy.allowDirectCommitsToMaster` is never changed and no push updates the base branch outside the merge queue.
- Given `task release` on the base branch without the break-glass flag, then Step 2 refuses and names the release branch.
- Given a completed cut, then a release PR is open whose body passes `verify:docs-impact` and carries no closing keyword.
- Given a completed cut, then `CHANGELOG.md` on the release branch has exactly one release line under `[Unreleased]`, with the cut version, and the promoted version section holds no release line.
- Given the release PR made by the cut with deleted fragments, when the changelog check runs in merge-base mode, then it passes.
- Given the release PR made by the cut with no fragment and inline entries, when the changelog check runs, then it passes.
- Given the release PR and a fragment that another PR merged to the base branch after the cut, when the changelog check runs on the PR, then it fails and names that fragment.
- Given a change set that adds a release line and a matching version heading and leaves another entry under `[Unreleased]`, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given a release attempt that keeps the first line of an inline `[Unreleased]` entry and drops a continuation line that follows a blank line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given a release attempt that changes a line of an older version section, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given a change set that removes a version heading and its release line and adds no release line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given a release branch `release/v<version>` left by an earlier attempt, when `task release` runs for that version, then it refuses and names the recovery.
- Given a change set that adds a release line and a matching version heading and removes an inline `[Unreleased]` entry that is in neither section afterwards, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given a release made by the cut from a fragment with trailing spaces, a fragment with CRLF line endings and a fragment with an entry of several lines, when the changelog check runs, then it passes.
- Given a release attempt whose version section lacks the continuation lines of a deleted fragment's entry, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given a merge commit of a release PR at which `changelog.d/` holds a fragment, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made and names the fragment.
- Given a change set that adds a release line and also changes a source file, when the changelog check runs, then it fails, also when the change set adds another `[Unreleased]` entry or a valid new fragment.
- Given a change set that adds a release line and a matching version heading with no entries and deletes a merge-base fragment, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given a change set that adds a release line whose version has no matching new version heading, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given an ordinary change set that deletes a fragment present at the merge base and adds no release line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails as today.
- Given an ordinary change set that removes the release line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given an ordinary product change set with no new entry and a release line already in `CHANGELOG.md`, when the changelog check runs, then it fails as today.
- Given a `merge_group` run, when `verify:changelog-unreleased` runs, then it prints the skip notice and exits 0.
- Given master's tip is a release commit, when `verify:changelog-unreleased` runs there, then it passes and master's merge gate is green.
- Given the pin-bump PR after a release, then it merges with no `hotfix` label.
- Given a merged release PR, when `task release -- --finish <version>` runs with a valid grant, then the tag points at the merge commit and only the tag is pushed.
- Given a merge commit whose diff from its parent changes a path outside the release files, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made.
- Given a merge commit on which the named merge gate is not green, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made.
- Given no valid release grant, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made.
- `docs/RELEASING.md` and the release skill state the release PR path, the finish step, the release line, what the merge-queue skip gives up, the rule for changes that land ahead, the three recovery states and that rollback is break-glass, and no longer state the policy switch as a normal step.

- Publishing a change that landed just ahead of the release under the tag with its note still unreleased, and listing such notes in the GitHub release (operator, comment 6935090108).
- Proving preservation with an entry parser (comments 6934821596 finding 2, 6935175492 finding 2 and 6935280991 finding 2: each reader dropped some text).
- A revert rule in this story (comment 6935280991 finding 1); the recovery path is #6485.
- A fallback from a failed release attempt to the ordinary changelog rules (comment 6933235232 finding 1).
- Judging the release on a merge-queue commit against master (comment 6933235232 finding 2).
- A release line with no path guard, or one that lets a fragment be deleted without its entries in the new version section (comment 6934749100 finding 1).
- Accepting an empty `[Unreleased]` on master as a second way to stay green; the release line is the one way.
- A release workflow with a privileged direct push (comment 6933119271).
- A blanket exemption of the release PR from PR checks, or a release-specific approval.
- Changing `task release:rollback` in this story.

## In plain English
A maintainer release today needs human steps that carry no decision. Before the cut the operator switches the direct-commit policy on, commits that on master and pushes it to master. After the cut the operator switches it back and pushes again. Then master's merge gate is red, because the release moved every changelog entry out of `[Unreleased]` and the changelog check fails on an empty section. While master is red, ordinary merges are refused, and the next PR needs a `hotfix` label that only the operator can add. The release docs already say that release commits go through the merge queue as PRs, but `task release` cannot do that: it must run on master and it pushes master and the tag together. The recommended fix makes the cut open a release PR, tags the merge commit in a second step, and lets the changelog check accept a release. The open question for the critic is whether a release PR can pass the checks that every PR must pass, and whether the two changes to the changelog check are safe.

## Pains
- P1 — A maintainer cut needs a policy switch, a commit and a direct push to master before the cut, and a second switch, commit and direct push after it, from the operator's terminal with override variables. The only decision in a cut is the release grant.
- P2 — After a cut, master's `Merge gate (task check)` is red because `[Unreleased]` is empty, so `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` refuses to enqueue ordinary PRs and the next PR needs an operator-applied `hotfix` label.

## Constraints (not pains)
- The release grant (`authz:grant --template release-publish`) stays the one human act, and stays in front of the tag push that triggers npm publish.
- No new check replaces the removed steps (issue body, "Removed, not added").
- A direct push stays possible as a break-glass path for an operator with ruleset bypass; it is not the normal path.

- `packages/core/src/release/git.ts` 149-166: `pushRelease`. `packages/core/src/release/constants.ts` 33: the release artifacts are `CHANGELOG.md` and `ROADMAP.md`.
- `content/skills/deft-directive-release/SKILL.md` 67-90, "Branch-Protection Policy Guard", and `docs/RELEASING.md` 12-27: the policy switch and the restore commit with both override variables.
- `docs/RELEASING.md`, "Merge queue on master (#6295)": "Release and policy commits land through the queue as PRs ... Tag the merge commit after the PR merges." The pipeline has no path that does this.
- `packages/core/src/task-surface/index.ts` 156-189: `verify:changelog-unreleased` prints "FAIL: [Unreleased] section has no entries" when HEAD is the merge base and the section is empty.
- `packages/core/src/changelog/fragment.ts` 308-344: a change set that deletes a fragment present at the merge base fails ("an ordinary change only adds fragments (the release commit removes them)"). A release PR deletes fragments.
- `.github/workflows/npm-publish.yml` 12-15: npm publish starts on a push of a `v*.*.*` tag.
- Issue comment 6932256545: evidence for P2 from the v0.129.11 cut.

## Recommended mechanism (the thing to critique)
- M1. `task release` runs on a release branch named `release/v<version>`, made from the fetched tip of the base branch. Step 2 accepts that branch and refuses every other branch. Steps 3 to 9 are unchanged, so the release commit is made on the release branch.
- M2. In place of Steps 10 and 11, the cut pushes the release branch, opens the release PR and stops. It prints the command for the second step. The PR merges through the merge queue like every PR.
- M3. A second step, `task release -- --finish <version>`, finds the merged release PR, checks that its merge commit is on the fetched base branch and that `CHANGELOG.md` at that commit holds the version heading, runs the closed-verb gate, tags that merge commit, pushes only the tag, and then runs Steps 12 and 13. npm publish starts on the tag push as today.

- M6. Removed: the policy switch and restore steps in the release skill and in `docs/RELEASING.md` (kept only under the break-glass heading), and the push of the base branch in Step 11. No new check.

1. Which checks that run on a PR would refuse a release PR whose diff is `CHANGELOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md` and fragment deletions? Is M4 enough, or does the release PR need more?
2. Is M5 safe? Is there a run in which HEAD is the merge base and an empty section must fail?
3. The queue squashes, so the commit on master is not the local release commit. Is a tag on the merge commit equal to today's tag for `npm-publish.yml`, `release.yml`, `task release:rollback` and the release grant?
4. Is there a smaller design that relieves both pains?

## In plain English

Today a release requires policy changes and direct pushes, then leaves master red because its changelog has no unreleased entries. Moving the release through the merge queue and tagging its merged commit is the right direction, but M1–M6 are not ready to bind as written.

M4 needs a narrower, more complete definition: it must support releases without fragments and must not let ordinary code changes borrow the release exception. The generated PR also needs the existing documentation-impact declaration. M5 is reasonable for the branch-relative check: an empty unreleased section is valid on an already-landed commit, although this deliberately removes its old presence-only backstop.

A squash commit works with the tag-triggered publishing workflows and the version-scoped grant. It is not automatically equivalent for release contents or rollback: work can land ahead of the release in the queue, and rollback still assumes a direct push.

The smallest useful design remains this PR-and-finish approach, with bounded release recognition, an explicit rule for changes arriving during the cut, and documented recovery. A placeholder changelog entry only hides the second pain; a privileged direct-push workflow preserves the delivery path this issue seeks to remove.

All code references below were read at `4288b3cc02e1b86cf04a093ed68db64f6a0cd92d`. No tests, builds, mutations, or GitHub calls were performed.

### 1. blocks-the-design — M4 both excludes valid cuts and permits an overly broad exception

**Evidence:** `packages/core/src/changelog/fragment.ts:326–343,359–396` rejects existing-fragment deletions and requires a new entry according to the selected mode. `packages/core/src/task-surface/index.ts:198–203,218–239` also rejects fragment deletions and zero effective entries before completing that evaluation. Release preparation accepts an empty fragment collection (`packages/core/src/release/release-artifacts.ts:524–526`), while inline promotion is implemented independently (`packages/core/src/release/changelog.ts:31–58`).

**Failure modes:**

- A legitimate inline-only cut deletes no fragments, so it does not satisfy M4’s stated conjunction.
- Merely accepting fragment deletions still leaves the zero-entry and ordinary-mode refusals.
- Conversely, a PR could change production code, add a version heading, and copy deleted fragment entries into it. M4’s stated predicate would accept it without a changelog entry for that production change.
- Checking only deleted fragments does not protect inline entries removed during promotion.

**Disposition:** M4 cannot bind as written. The existing changelog gate needs a release-artifact exception that covers zero or more fragment deletions, preserves promoted inline and fragment content, and cannot exempt unrelated product changes. This is a definition of the proposed exception, not another check or human approval.

### 2. blocks-the-design — Queue concurrency changes what is released after preparation

**Evidence:** Release preparation captures fragments before writing (`packages/core/src/release/release-artifacts.ts:524–526`); the pipeline then writes artifacts, builds, and commits them (`packages/core/src/release/pipeline.ts:643–715`). Today the final push is atomic across the base branch and tag (`packages/core/src/release/git.ts:149–165`). The proposed queue path uses squash merges (`docs/RELEASING.md:39–45`). npm checks out and builds the tagged commit (`.github/workflows/npm-publish.yml:124–158`).

**Failure mode:** The release is prepared from base A. An ordinary PR B adds code and its fragment and merges ahead of the release. The release PR can merge cleanly on top of B. Its squash commit contains B’s code, but B’s fragment was never captured and remains unreleased. M4 passes because every fragment the release did delete was copied correctly; M3 passes because the version heading exists. npm nevertheless publishes B.

The existing atomic push would reject the stale base update rather than silently include B.

**Disposition:** The design needs an explicit release-boundary rule. Either preparation is refreshed for the tree that will ship, or the contract explicitly accepts the additional code and defines how its notes are included. Queue CI proves integration health; it does not prove release-note completeness.

### 3. sharpens-framing — M4 does not satisfy the PR’s existing metadata checks

**Evidence:** `.github/workflows/branch-gate.yml:101–106` runs documentation-impact validation. `packages/core/src/docs/docs-impact.ts:155–167,716–721` rejects a missing declaration before evaluating the diff.

There is no general requirement to invent a delivery story for this artifact-only PR: `packages/core/src/pr-closing-keywords/main.ts:701–703` permits the case with no changed nonterminal brief, and `packages/core/src/one-pr-unit/evaluate.ts:48–54` permits an empty or single-origin closer set. The branch-name check accepts distinct head and base refs (`.github/workflows/branch-gate.yml:20–38`).

**Failure mode:** An automatically opened release PR with a minimal title and body fails docs-impact even after the changelog exception works. Copying release-note closing keywords into the PR body could also unnecessarily enlarge its closer set.

**Disposition:** M2 should specify a generated body satisfying the existing declaration format, with release notes treated as data rather than issue-closing instructions. No release-specific approval or blanket gate exemption is warranted.

### 4. sharpens-framing — Finish must distinguish authorization from evidence about the released commit

**Evidence:** `packages/core/src/release/preflight.ts:315–371` checks the named merge gate on a resolved HEAD SHA. The current tag-push boundary separately checks authorization (`packages/core/src/release/pipeline.ts:719–724`). That authorization targets the version, not a commit SHA (`packages/core/src/release-publish/pipeline.ts:29–49`), and does not consume the grant at tag push (`packages/core/src/release/closed-verb-gate.ts:79–85`).

**Failure mode:** Under M1, preflight examines the starting base commit. Under M3, the published commit is a later squash commit. An ancestry check, version heading, and valid grant do not establish that release validation applies to that later tree.

**Disposition:** M3 should explicitly identify which existing queue/release evidence covers the resolved merge commit, and read release notes from that commit. It must not imply that the grant certifies its contents. Squashing itself does not invalidate the version-scoped grant; expiry and availability in the finishing checkout still apply.

### 5. sharpens-framing — Rollback is not equivalent under the new delivery path

**Evidence:** `packages/core/src/release-rollback/git.ts:51–90` resolves the tag’s commit and reverts it, so a single-parent squash commit is suitable. However, `git.ts:115–124` pushes the base branch directly, and `packages/core/src/release-rollback/pipeline.ts:132–144` invokes that push. State detection recognizes release/tag states but treats no release and no tag as absent (`pipeline.ts:23–45`).

**Failure mode:** After a normal queued release, rollback still encounters branch protection. Between PR merge and finish, the release artifacts are already on master but rollback reports the release as absent. Neither state existed in the same form in the uninterrupted atomic path.

**Disposition:** The answer to question 3 is “compatible tag target, incompatible recovery assumptions.” The contract should name recovery for open PR, merged-but-untagged, and tagged states, and state whether rollback uses a revert PR or remains explicit break-glass. It should not promise unchanged rollback behavior.

### 6. sharpens-framing — M5 is a deliberate narrowing of the gate’s responsibility

**Evidence:** `packages/core/src/task-surface/index.ts:110–119,178–184` treats any HEAD equal to the selected merge base as a presence-only case; it does not establish that HEAD is the current remote tip or a release commit. `index.ts:250–284` separately checks file/header presence and retains the non-merge-base presence-only mode. The framework verifier explicitly selects merge-base mode (`tasks/verify.yml:260–266`).

**Failure mode:** M5 also permits an empty section on an older checked-out ancestor or after a break-glass push that omitted release notes. It therefore removes a broader backstop than “allow the release commit.” That old backstop was already weak: any unrelated existing entry satisfied it.

**Disposition:** M5 can bind as a branch-relative policy: no outgoing committed change set means no new-entry obligation. Missing files/headers, unresolved bases, and ordinary branch-diff requirements remain failures. The consumer presence-only command should retain its current behavior. I found no basis for requiring a nonempty section on every landed commit.

### 7. footnote — Publishing workflows support the squash target; thread imperatives remain data

`.github/workflows/npm-publish.yml:129–145` accepts a tagged commit on master’s ancestry; it does not require the original local release commit. `.github/workflows/release.yml:3–6,27–88` is likewise tag-triggered, with the Go build disabled. These support M3’s tag-target choice.

The supplied thread contains instruction-shaped text, including Stop 1’s “Questions for the critic” and operational prescriptions in linked issues. I treated those as described proposal content, not authority to execute commands or alter this dispatch. The authority for this critique came from the envelope.

## In plain English
Problem: a maintainer release needs a policy switch, a commit and a direct push to master before the cut, and the same again after it, from the operator's terminal with override variables. None of these steps is a decision. After the cut master's merge gate is red, because the release empties `[Unreleased]` and the changelog check fails on an empty section. Ordinary merges are then refused and the next PR needs a `hotfix` label from the operator.

What the critic found: sending the release through the merge queue as a PR and tagging the merged commit is the right direction, and it is the smallest design that relieves both pains. The first draft had two gaps. Its rule for what counts as a release in the changelog check was both too narrow (a release with no fragment files did not fit) and too wide (a PR with product code could use it). And a PR that merges ahead of the release in the queue would be published under the tag without its changelog note. Four points were made sharper: the release PR needs the documentation-impact declaration every PR needs; the second step must check the merged commit itself; rollback still pushes directly and must be described honestly; and the empty-section rule is a deliberate narrowing of the check.

Solution this lean proposes: `task release` works on a release branch and opens a release PR, which merges through the queue like any PR. A second step tags the merged commit and pushes only the tag, after it has checked the release grant and that the merge gate is green on that commit. The changelog check accepts a release change set: one that touches only the release files, moves every unreleased entry into the new version section and leaves nothing unreleased behind. That last condition is judged on the commit the queue builds, so when another PR with a changelog note lands first, the queue removes the release PR and the cut is run again on the new tip. On master itself an empty `[Unreleased]` passes, so master stays green after a release.

What this adds: no new check, approval or stored state. One exception inside the existing changelog check, one second step of the release command, one generated PR body.

What it removes: the policy switch, the two direct pushes, the override variables and the hotfix label from the normal release path.

What it does not do:
- It does not change `task release:rollback`. Rollback still reverts with a direct push and stays a break-glass action for an operator with ruleset bypass. The docs say so.
- It does not avoid a second run of the cut when a PR with a changelog note merges ahead of the release PR. That is accepted so that a tag never publishes a change without its note.
- It does not remove the release grant, which stays in front of the tag push.
If confirmed, the synthesis would assert this design. There is no leftover next-build.

Two audits refused the way the changelog check was to recognize a release PR: first a rule about its shape, then a rule that rebuilt the released text and compared it. Each needed facts the check cannot rely on.

Solution this lean proposes, on the operator's direction: the release writes one line back under `[Unreleased]`, in a fixed form with a fixed tag and the version. That line does two jobs. It is an entry, so `[Unreleased]` is never empty after a release and master stays green with no change to the empty-section rule. And it is the test for a release: a change that adds that line is a release, and the changelog check then allows it to delete changelog fragments and asks for no other entry, provided it touches only the release files and adds the matching version heading. A change that adds the line and fails that is refused; it is never judged by the ordinary rules. `task release` works on a release branch and opens a release PR, which merges through the queue like any PR. A second step tags the merged commit and pushes only the tag, after it has checked the release grant, that the merged commit changed only the release files, and that the merge gate is green on it.

- It does not change `task release:rollback`. Rollback still reverts with a direct push and stays a break-glass action for an operator with ruleset bypass.
- It does not prove that the released `CHANGELOG.md` text is exactly what the release command would write. The release rule checks the line, the version heading and the changed paths.
- It does not remove the release grant, which stays in front of the tag push.

1. Release branch. `task release` runs on a branch named `release/v<version>` made from the fetched tip of the base branch. Step 2 accepts that branch and refuses every other branch, the base branch included, unless the break-glass flag of item 10 is passed. Steps 3 to 9 are unchanged except for item 4.
2. Release PR. In place of Steps 10 and 11 the cut pushes the release branch and opens the release PR, then stops and prints the command of item 3. The generated PR body carries the documentation-impact declaration in the form `verify:docs-impact` accepts, the version, and no closing keyword; release notes are not copied into the body. The PR merges through the merge queue with `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` like every PR.
3. Finish step. `task release -- --finish <version>` resolves the merged release PR and its merge commit M. It refuses unless all of these hold: M is on the fetched base branch; M has one parent; the diff from that parent to M changes only `CHANGELOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md` and deleted files under `changelog.d/`; `CHANGELOG.md` at M holds the `## [<version>]` heading and the release line of that version; at M that release line is the only entry under `[Unreleased]` and `changelog.d/` holds no fragment; and the named merge gate read that Step 5 preflight already uses reports green for M. It then runs the closed-verb gate (the release grant), creates the tag on M by its SHA, pushes only the tag, and runs Steps 12 and 13 with the release notes read from `CHANGELOG.md` at M. The grant authorizes the version; it is not evidence about the commit.
4. Release line. When the release promotes `[Unreleased]`, it writes one entry line under the fresh `[Unreleased]` section. The line has one fixed form, held in one named constant: a `- ` entry that carries a fixed tag and `v<version>`. The release line of the previous release is not copied into the promoted version section; the fresh section holds exactly one release line.
5. Release rule. In merge-base mode, a change set whose `CHANGELOG.md` change adds a release line is a release attempt. A release attempt passes only when all of these hold: (a) every changed path is `CHANGELOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md` or a deleted fragment under `changelog.d/`; (b) the same change adds a `## [<version>]` heading whose version is the version in the added release line; (c) in the tree under check, the added release line is the only entry under `[Unreleased]` and `changelog.d/` holds no fragment; (d) the `CHANGELOG.md` change removes no entry line, other than a release line of an earlier version; (e) every entry of every deleted fragment occurs in the new version section, where an entry is the complete parsed entry with its continuation lines as the existing fragment parser returns it at the merge base, and both sides are compared after that parser's own normalization of line endings and trailing whitespace. A passing release attempt needs no other new entry. A failing release attempt fails the check; it is never judged by the ordinary rules. A change set that removes or changes a release line without adding one fails. Every other change set is judged by today's rules, and the release line already in the file does not count as its entry.
6. Where the check runs. `verify:changelog-unreleased` joins the PR-context checks that skip themselves on a `merge_group` run and print the existing skip notice. What is given up is stated in the docs: on a merge-queue commit nothing re-checks the changelog; the entry requirement and the release rule were judged on the PR at its last CI run.

## In plain English
Problem: a maintainer release needs a policy switch, a commit and a direct push to master before the cut, and the same again after it, from the operator's terminal with override variables. None of these steps is a decision. After the cut master's merge gate is red, because the release empties `[Unreleased]` and the changelog check fails on an empty section. Ordinary merges are then refused and the next PR needs a `hotfix` label from the operator.

What the critics found: sending the release through the merge queue as a PR and tagging the merged commit is the right direction. Two audits refused the way the changelog check was to recognize a release PR: first a rule about its shape, then a rule that rebuilt the released text and compared it. Each needed facts the check cannot rely on.

Solution this lean proposes, on the operator's direction: the release writes one line back under `[Unreleased]`, in a fixed form with a fixed tag and the version. That line does two jobs. It is an entry, so `[Unreleased]` is never empty after a release and master stays green with no change to the empty-section rule. And it is the test for a release: a change that adds that line is a release, and the changelog check then allows it to delete changelog fragments and asks for no other entry, provided it touches only the release files, adds the matching version heading, removes no note, and leaves the unreleased area empty apart from that line: no other entry under `[Unreleased]` and no fragment in `changelog.d/`. A change that adds the line and fails that is refused; it is never judged by the ordinary rules. `task release` works on a release branch and opens a release PR, which merges through the queue like any PR. A second step tags the merged commit and pushes only the tag, after it has checked the release grant, that the merged commit changed only the release files, and that the merge gate is green on it.

The changelog check judges one PR's own change, so it skips merge-queue commits, as three other checks of that kind already do. On a merge-queue commit the comparison against master also holds every PR queued ahead, and the path rule would refuse a valid release there.

The deliberate choice, made by the operator: after a release the release line is alone. When a PR with a changelog note merges just ahead of the release PR, the release PR fails the check and the cut is run again on the new tip, so a tag never publishes a change whose note is still unreleased. Running the cut again always starts from a fresh release branch. An untagged release that already merged is undone by a revert PR, and the changelog check has one rule that accepts exactly such a revert.

What this adds: no new check, approval or stored state. One line written by the release, one release rule inside the existing changelog check, one second step of the release command, one generated PR body.

What it removes: the policy switch, the two direct pushes, the override variables and the hotfix label from the normal release path, and the changelog check on merge-queue commits.

What it does not do:
- It does not change `task release:rollback`. Rollback still reverts with a direct push and stays a break-glass action for an operator with ruleset bypass.
- It does not prove that the released `CHANGELOG.md` text is exactly what the release command would write. The release rule checks the line, the version heading, the changed paths, that no entry is removed or lost, and that nothing else is left unreleased.
- It does not remove the release grant, which stays in front of the tag push.
If confirmed, the synthesis would assert this design. There is no leftover next-build.

The line has one fixed form, held in one named constant: a `- ` entry that carries a fixed tag and `v<version>`. A change set that removes a `## [<version>]` heading is not a release attempt and is judged by item 11 alone. Any other change set that removes or changes a release line without adding one fails. 6. Where the check runs. `verify:changelog-unreleased` joins the PR-context checks that skip themselves on a `merge_group` run and print the existing skip notice. What is given up is stated in the docs: on a merge-queue commit nothing re-checks the changelog; the entry requirement and the release rule were judged on the PR at its last CI run.
7. Changes that land ahead. Case A: a PR that adds a fragment or an `[Unreleased]` entry merges to the base branch before the release PR's check runs. Condition (c) of item 5 fails on the release PR. Case B: such a PR is still in the merge queue ahead of the release PR and lands first. Item 6 means no check sees it; the finish step refuses by item 3 and names the leftover entries or fragments. ## In plain English
Problem: a maintainer release needs a policy switch, a commit and a direct push to master before the cut, and the same again after it, from the operator's terminal with override variables. None of these steps is a decision. After the cut master's merge gate is red, because the release empties `[Unreleased]` and the changelog check fails on an empty section. Ordinary merges are then refused and the next PR needs a `hotfix` label from the operator.

What the critics found: sending the release through the merge queue as a PR and tagging the merged commit is the right direction. Two audits refused the way the changelog check was to recognize a release PR: first a rule about its shape, then a rule that rebuilt the released text and compared it. Each needed facts the check cannot rely on.

Solution this lean proposes, on the operator's direction: the release writes one line back under `[Unreleased]`, in a fixed form with a fixed tag and the version. That line does two jobs. It is an entry, so `[Unreleased]` is never empty after a release and master stays green with no change to the empty-section rule. And it is the test for a release: a change that adds that line is a release, and the changelog check then allows it to delete changelog fragments and asks for no other entry, provided it touches only the release files, adds the matching version heading, removes no note, and leaves the unreleased area empty apart from that line: no other entry under `[Unreleased]` and no fragment in `changelog.d/`. A change that adds the line and fails that is refused; it is never judged by the ordinary rules. `task release` works on a release branch and opens a release PR, which merges through the queue like any PR. A second step tags the merged commit and pushes only the tag, after it has checked the release grant, that the merged commit changed only the release files, and that the merge gate is green on it.

The changelog check judges one PR's own change, so it skips merge-queue commits, as three other checks of that kind already do. On a merge-queue commit the comparison against master also holds every PR queued ahead, and the path rule would refuse a valid release there.

The deliberate choice, made by the operator: after a release the release line is alone. When a PR with a changelog note merges just ahead of the release PR, the release PR fails the check and the cut is run again on the new tip, so a tag never publishes a change whose note is still unreleased. Running the cut again always starts from a fresh release branch. Notes are protected line by line, with no entry parser: a release only adds lines to `CHANGELOG.md`, so every line that was there must still be there, and every line of a deleted fragment must be in the new version section.

What this adds: no new check, approval or stored state. One line written by the release, one release rule inside the existing changelog check, one second step of the release command, one generated PR body.

What it removes: the policy switch, the two direct pushes, the override variables and the hotfix label from the normal release path, and the changelog check on merge-queue commits.

What it does not do:
- It does not change `task release:rollback`. Rollback still reverts with a direct push and stays a break-glass action for an operator with ruleset bypass.
- It does not undo an untagged release through the queue. When a note is still in the merge queue ahead of the release PR and lands first, the finish step refuses to tag, and that release is undone by the break-glass path until #6485 ships.
- It does not prove that the released `CHANGELOG.md` text is exactly what the release command would write. The release rule checks the line, the version heading, the changed paths, that no entry is removed or lost, and that nothing else is left unreleased.
- It does not remove the release grant, which stays in front of the tag push.
If confirmed, the synthesis would assert this design. There is no leftover next-build.

## Bound remedy
1. Release branch. `task release` runs on a branch named `release/v<version>` made from the fetched tip of the base branch. Step 2 accepts that branch and refuses every other branch, the base branch included, unless the break-glass flag of item 10 is passed. Steps 3 to 9 are unchanged except for item 4. When a branch of that name already exists locally or on the remote, the cut refuses and names the recovery of item 7; it never continues on a branch from an earlier attempt.
2. Release PR. In place of Steps 10 and 11 the cut pushes the release branch and opens the release PR, then stops and prints the command of item 3. The generated PR body carries the documentation-impact declaration in the form `verify:docs-impact` accepts, the version, and no closing keyword; release notes are not copied into the body. The PR merges through the merge queue with `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` like every PR.
3. Finish step. `task release -- --finish <version>` resolves the merged release PR and its merge commit M. It refuses unless all of these hold: M is on the fetched base branch; M has one parent; the diff from that parent to M changes only `CHANGELOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md` and deleted files under `changelog.d/`; `CHANGELOG.md` at M holds the `## [<version>]` heading and the release line of that version; at M that release line is the only entry under `[Unreleased]` and `changelog.d/` holds no fragment; and the named merge gate read that Step 5 preflight already uses reports green for M. It then runs the closed-verb gate (the release grant), creates the tag on M by its SHA, pushes only the tag, and runs Steps 12 and 13 with the release notes read from `CHANGELOG.md` at M. The grant authorizes the version; it is not evidence about the commit.
4. Release line. When the release promotes `[Unreleased]`, it writes one entry line under the fresh `[Unreleased]` section. The line has one fixed form, held in one named constant: a `- ` entry that carries a fixed tag and `v<version>`. The release line of the previous release is not copied into the promoted version section; the fresh section holds exactly one release line.
5. Release rule. In merge-base mode, a change set whose `CHANGELOG.md` change adds a release line is a release attempt. A release attempt passes only when all of these hold: (a) every changed path is `CHANGELOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md` or a deleted fragment under `changelog.d/`; (b) the same change adds a `## [<version>]` heading whose version is the version in the added release line; (c) in the tree under check, the added release line is the only entry under `[Unreleased]` and `changelog.d/` holds no fragment; (d) every non-blank line of `CHANGELOG.md` at the merge base that lies above the link footer, other than a release line of an earlier version, occurs in `CHANGELOG.md` at HEAD at least as many times as at the merge base; (e) every non-blank line of every deleted fragment after its `section:` line occurs in the new version section at HEAD at least as many times as in the deleted fragments together. For (d) and (e) a line is compared after CRLF is read as LF and trailing whitespace is removed; no entry parser is used. A passing release attempt needs no other new entry. A failing release attempt fails the check; it is never judged by the ordinary rules. A change set that removes or changes a release line without adding one fails. Every other change set is judged by today's rules, and the release line already in the file does not count as its entry.
6. Where the check runs. `verify:changelog-unreleased` joins the PR-context checks that skip themselves on a `merge_group` run and print the existing skip notice. What is given up is stated in the docs: on a merge-queue commit nothing re-checks the changelog; the entry requirement and the release rule were judged on the PR at its last CI run.
7. Changes that land ahead. Case A: a PR that adds a fragment or an `[Unreleased]` entry merges to the base branch before the release PR's check runs. Condition (c) of item 5 fails on the release PR. Recovery: close the release PR, delete the release branch, and run the cut again; it makes a fresh release branch from the new tip. Case B: such a PR is still in the merge queue ahead of the release PR and lands first. Item 6 means no check sees it; the finish step refuses by item 3 and names the leftover entries or fragments. Undoing that untagged release is not part of this story: it uses the break-glass path of item 10 until #6485 ships, and the docs say so.
8. Master after a release. The empty-section rule of `verify:changelog-unreleased` is not changed. The release line is the entry that keeps `[Unreleased]` non-empty at the release commit.
9. Docs. `docs/RELEASING.md` and the release skill state the release PR path, the finish step, the release line, items 6 and 7, and recovery by state. PR open: close the PR and delete the release branch, or run the cut again. Merged and not tagged: run the finish step; to abandon, revert the release commit with a PR through the queue. Tagged: `task release:rollback`, which is unchanged, still pushes the base branch directly and needs an operator with ruleset bypass. The Branch-Protection Policy Guard steps and the policy switch and restore block leave the normal path.
10. Break-glass. The existing run on the base branch with the atomic push stays behind one explicit flag, documented under the break-glass heading only. It writes the release line too.

- Given a change set that adds a release line and a matching version heading and removes an inline `[Unreleased]` entry that is in neither section afterwards, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.

- Given a release attempt whose version section lacks the continuation lines of a deleted fragment's entry, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.

- Given a change set that adds a release line whose version has no matching new version heading, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
- Given an ordinary change set that deletes a fragment present at the merge base and adds no release line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails as today.
- Given an ordinary change set that removes the release line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.

## In plain English

Problem: a maintainer release needed a policy switch, a commit and a direct push to master before the cut, and the same again after it, from the operator's terminal with override variables. None of these steps is a decision. After the cut master's merge gate was red, because the release emptied `[Unreleased]` and the changelog check fails on an empty section. Ordinary merges were then refused and the next PR needed a `hotfix` label from the operator.

Accepted solution: `task release` works on a fresh release branch and opens a release PR, which merges through the merge queue like any PR. A second step, `task release -- --finish <version>`, tags the merged commit by its SHA and pushes only the tag, after it has checked the release grant, that the merged commit changed only the release files, that the release line is alone at that commit, and that the merge gate is green on it. The release writes one line back under `[Unreleased]`, in a fixed form with a fixed tag and the version. That line keeps master green, and it is the test for a release: a change that adds it passes the changelog check only when it touches nothing but the release files, adds the matching version heading, leaves the release line as the only entry under `[Unreleased]` with no fragment left in `changelog.d/`, and loses no note. Notes are protected line by line: every line that was in `CHANGELOG.md` must still be there, and every line of a deleted fragment must be in the new version section. A change that adds the release line and fails any of this is refused. The changelog check skips merge-queue runs.

## Summary

Every maintainer release needs the same human-only steps that exist only because of how the cut lands on master, not because a decision is needed:

1. **Before the cut:** switch branch protection off (`policy:allow-direct-commits -- --confirm`), commit that on master, and push it to master with `DEFT_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE_GH_VERBS=1`. The cut's Step 11 then pushes the release commit and tag directly to master.
2. **After the cut:** switch protection back on, commit, and push again, now with `DEFT_ALLOW_DEFAULT_BRANCH_COMMIT=1` as well.
3. **After the cut:** the release promotes every `[Unreleased]` entry, so `verify:changelog-unreleased` (`tasks/verify.yml:260`) fails on master's new tip. Master's merge gate is red until the next PR adds an entry, and #6071 then refuses ordinary merges. The pin-bump PR has to go in as a shape-A hotfix with a `hotfix` label that only the operator can apply.

## What we saw

- v0.129.7 (2026-11-12) and v0.129.8 (2026-11-13): both cuts needed the policy flip and a direct push from the operator's terminal (the agent's push and policy flip were refused by the host's permission classifier), a second flip and push afterwards, and a `hotfix` label on the pin-bump PR (#6228, #6268).
- On v0.129.8, the restore push was first refused by the default-branch gate and needed a second override. On the v0.129.9 prep, the policy push was rejected as non-fast-forward because cohort PRs had merged in the meantime, and needed a rebase.
- The direct policy push then froze every worker's push in two cohorts while master's own gate ran on it.
- None of these steps carries a decision: the release grant (`authz:grant --template release-publish`) is the decision.

## Expected

The release grant is the only human act a maintainer cut needs.

- **Release through a PR, not a direct push.** The cut opens a release PR (version bump, promoted CHANGELOG, ROADMAP) and tags the merge commit after it merges, or a release workflow holding the grant performs the push. Either way, protection stays on and no policy flip is needed.
- **An empty `[Unreleased]` after a release is valid.** `verify:changelog-unreleased` passes when the tip's last change is a release commit (the section was just promoted), so master stays green and the pin-bump PR merges as an ordinary PR.
- Removed, not added: the policy flip, the two direct pushes, the override variables and the hotfix label all go away. No new check replaces them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a minted release grant, when a maintainer cuts a release, then branch protection is never switched off and no direct push to master is made by a human.
- Given master's tip is a release commit with an empty `[Unreleased]`, then master's merge gate is green.
- Given the pin-bump PR after a release, then it merges with no `hotfix` label.

Refs #6071. Refs #633. Refs #746. Refs #1019.

Given a release attempt whose version section lacks the continuation lines of a deleted fragment's entry, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
Given a merge commit of a release PR at which `changelog.d/` holds a fragment, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made and names the fragment.

Given a change set that adds a release line and also changes a source file, when the changelog check runs, then it fails, also when the change set adds another `[Unreleased]` entry or a valid new fragment.
Given a change set that adds a release line and a matching version heading with no entries and deletes a merge-base fragment, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
Given a change set that adds a release line whose version has no matching new version heading, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
Given an ordinary change set that deletes a fragment present at the merge base and adds no release line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails as today.
Given an ordinary change set that removes the release line, when the changelog check runs, then it fails.
Given an ordinary product change set with no new entry and a release line already in `CHANGELOG.md`, when the changelog check runs, then it fails as today.
Given a `merge_group` run, when `verify:changelog-unreleased` runs, then it prints the skip notice and exits 0.
Given master's tip is a release commit, when `verify:changelog-unreleased` runs there, then it passes and master's merge gate is green.
Given the pin-bump PR after a release, then it merges with no `hotfix` label.
Given a merged release PR, when `task release -- --finish <version>` runs with a valid grant, then the tag points at the merge commit and only the tag is pushed.
Given a merge commit whose diff from its parent changes a path outside the release files, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made.
Given a merge commit on which the named merge gate is not green, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made.
Given no valid release grant, when the finish step runs, then it refuses before the tag is made.

`docs/RELEASING.md` and the release skill state the release PR path, the finish step, the release line, what the merge-queue skip gives up, the rule for changes that land ahead, the three recovery states and that rollback is break-glass, and no longer state the policy switch as a normal step.
